title: Will Voters Punish Politicians for Data Centers? Ask Ohio and Michigan
source_used: Long excerpt of the WSJ article reproduced by MishTalk (WSJ page itself returns HTTP 401)
key_facts: The WSJ says data-centre fights are mostly local but voters are demanding action from federal and state candidates; early voting starts within days and both parties are watching how far the issue reaches up the ballot.
In Pataskala, Ohio, east of Columbus, the city council in August rejected a 200-megawatt data center after resident opposition; opponents now push a charter amendment to block future ones.

A September Bowling Green State University survey of 1,000 likely Ohio voters found 70% saw data centers as bad for the environment and 69% as bad for home-energy costs; almost eight in ten favored a temporary construction pause.

A Michigan State University poll found more than two-thirds of Michigan respondents opposed local data centers; a national WSJ survey found 62% supported pausing development, 39% calling it a top priority.
In Ohio's Senate race, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who leads in recent polls, has made reining in data centers a core issue and his campaign calls Republican Sen. Jon Husted 'the face of data centers'.

In August the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that data centers are 'the anchor hanging around Husted's neck' and advised candidates to focus on utility costs; Husted backed a Ratepayer Protection Act that House Republicans passed and Senate Democrats blocked as ineffective.
Ohio has more than 200 data centers operating, under construction or planned.
quote_evidence: Many of the fights remain hyperlocal, having more to do with city councils than U.S. senators.

why_it_matters_hint: Anger over data-centre costs and land use is reaching Senate campaigns in two Midwest states.
notes: Read only the excerpt MishTalk reproduces from the WSJ (mostly the Ohio part and the Michigan poll line); the Michigan section of the WSJ article was not seen, so no Michigan detail beyond the poll is used. MishTalk's own commentary was ignored.
